The Domain Model

Users, tickets, comments, tags, and watchers — the entities this whole API exists to manage, and how they relate.

The system is a support ticketing app: customers submit tickets, agents get assigned to and comment on them, tickets carry tags for categorization, and users can watch a ticket to be notified when something happens on it. Six entities cover the whole thing:

  • User — one table for everyone, distinguished by a role: customer, agent, or admin. What a user can do and see depends entirely on this field, not on which table they're stored in.
  • Ticket — belongs to exactly one customer (1:M — a customer can have many tickets), and optionally to one assigned agent (also 1:M, on the same User table, via a second, separately-named foreign key).
  • Comment — belongs to exactly one Ticket and one author User (1:M on both).
  • Tag — a M:N relationship with Ticket, through a plain join table (TicketTag) that carries no data of its own beyond the link.
  • Watchers — also M:N between User and Ticket, but through a join table (TicketWatcher) that does carry its own data: a notifyOnComment flag, per watcher, per ticket.
  • Notification — belongs to one User (1:M); populated later by event listeners, not written directly by a controller.

None of this modeling is new to you — 1:M and M:N relationships are exactly what you already built in Laravel with Eloquent migrations and models. What's new is expressing the same relationships in Prisma's schema file (prisma/schema.prisma) instead of a series of migration files: one declarative file is the schema, rather than a sequence of changes that produce it.

// Figure 0.1: Ticket's two relations to User (prisma/schema.prisma, excerpt)
model Ticket {
  id              Int          @id @default(autoincrement())
  subject         String
  description     String       @db.Text
  status          TicketStatus @default(open)
  customerId      Int
  assignedAgentId Int?

  customer      User  @relation("CustomerTickets", fields: [customerId], references: [id])
  assignedAgent User? @relation("AssignedTickets", fields: [assignedAgentId], references: [id])
  comments      Comment[]
  tags          TicketTag[]
  watchers      TicketWatcher[]
}

Two named relations ("CustomerTickets", "AssignedTickets") on the same customer/assignedAgent fields are what make the dual User relationship possible at all — without a name on each, Prisma has no way to tell which foreign key belongs to which relation. assignedAgentId Int? (nullable) is what makes assignment optional: a ticket exists, and can be queried, before any agent picks it up.

This core shape stays fixed for the rest of the course — every lesson from here on builds on this model. It gets exactly one addition later (a single new column, to support a background job you haven't met yet), flagged clearly when that lesson introduces it — never a change to what's shown above.
